aa8e964eeccef16d.title: Hardening Agentic Web Populations Through Multi-Criterion Competitive Co-Evolution: Lessons from Wargame Strategy Optimization
aa8e964eeccef16d.text: Agents on the open web will face adversaries that keep adapting, so a defense that is only tested once will eventually be found and broken. We propose treating jailbreak attacks and safety guardrails as two populations that evolve against each other, rather than as a fixed attacker probing a fixed defense. This idea comes directly from wargame strategy optimization, where two-population competitive co-evolution with alternating evolution cycles and cross-play evaluation has already been shown to produce strategies that are robust to a moving opponent, and where a companion line of work has shown that the same machinery can measure how much competitive pressure a population must absorb. However, real-world applications can never rely on a single criterion as a key performance indicator, rather must use multiple conflicting criteria, such as, cost and efficiency. We describe how this mechanism transfers to language model safety, argue why the resulting multi-criteria, competitive and coevolutionary arms race is a genuinely networked, population-level problem rather than a two-agent toy setting, and lay out the open problems that stand between the wargame version of this idea and an agentic web version of it.

ac2fe67a1e81f207.title: Which technologies for which activity? A multi-case analysis of hybrid creative spaces
ac2fe67a1e81f207.text: Hybrid creative spaces combine physical, digital, and virtual environments to support creative work, yet research on creative spaces has focused largely on the physical built environment, while research on hybrid environments has emphasized technological systems without differentiating among creative activities. This study empirically elaborates a design-oriented framework that relates five creative-space types (personal, collaboration, making, presentation, and intermission) to the five TACIT dimensions of hybrid environments (Territoriality, Awareness, Control, Interaction, and Transitions). Using a multiple-case study, we analyzed 21 hybrid environments across workplace, education, conferencing, art, and laboratory settings. From these cases, 318 scenario-based analytical units were extracted, positioned within the framework, and abstracted into 54 recurring technological characteristics. The characteristics differed in emphasis across activities: personal activity included privacy and individual control, collaboration included co-presence and shared awareness, making included simulation, sensing, and automation, presentation included visual accessibility and facilitator support, and intermission included ambient display and serendipitous encounter. A few characteristics, such as linkage and remote connection, appeared in all five creative-space types, so their relevance cannot be tied to a single activity. Because the analysis is exploratory and relies largely on secondary documentation, it shows where characteristics were identified, not their effects. The study offers an activity-centered basis for analyzing and designing hybrid creative environments without treating technology as a generic add-on or assuming that particular technologies produce creativity.

b21421633eabfb0f.title: The Athlete as a Scientist of One: Agentic Bayesian Experimental Design for Individualized Physiology from Consumer Wearables
b21421633eabfb0f.text: Large language model (LLM) agents for personal health read wearable data and recommend, but do not learn about the individual in a way that can be audited or falsified. We present EpiCoach, an agentic system that treats one athlete, a cross-country mountain biker, as the subject of accountable N-of-1 science. Claims about the athlete live in an evidence-gated hypothesis registry: each must issue a probabilistic prediction about a future session before it occurs, and its belief moves only through computed evidence from a logged statistical fit. Predictions come from a mechanistic digital twin inferred from heart rate, GPS and barometric altitude: a lagged heart-rate response model, a fitness-fatigue model with learned time constants, and a latent technical-descending skill state, measured on discovered trail segments. The agent prescribes the next training week as a constrained experiment maximizing information gain subject to load and safety constraints, around two instrument rides. We evaluate the system two ways over eighteen months of data. A rolling-origin replay benchmark shows the twin beats standard forecasters on heart rate but not segment time, and the agentic loop matches a static model. A live prospective phase runs the weekly cycle: in its first three weeks the ledger sealed 20 predictions, scored 14, the descent forecast calibrated after one correction, the climb forecast pessimistic as the athlete improved, and the safety officer vetoed the agent twice. Every correction is preserved in the registry, a template for auditable, falsifiable personalization in digital health. We release the registry, benchmark and protocol.

bbc9b4d66e7e40f5.title: A Crowd-Audited Atlas of Implicit Bias in LLM-Powered Agents
bbc9b4d66e7e40f5.text: Prior work has shown that large language models (LLMs) express implicit biases in high-publicity, one-off decision scenarios such as hiring and intelligence assessment. However, as people increasingly employ autonomous, LLM-powered AI agents that make decisions on their behalf in doing day-to-day tasks, it is of critical importance that we understand how implicit biases, based on sociodemographic assumptions, emerge across a broad milieu of workaday decision scenarios. We used the 17 domains of daily activity in the American Time Use Survey (ATUS) to generate an atlas of 506 decision scenarios in which LLMs --- endowed with personas representing different races, gender identities, and political ideologies --- expressed significant implicit bias. Next, in a crowdsourced audit, 500 participants made 8,010 binary choices about which implicitly biased decision scenarios most deserved further review. We found that participants prioritized decision scenarios that had broad relevance (e.g., about food choices), were high stakes (e.g., about health), and where all members of a simulated sociodemographic group made unanimous decisions (because it was a clear indication of stereotyping). They were less swayed by the magnitude of an observed disparity or the specific ATUS domain the decision scenario represented. When examining the rationale behind their prioritization choices, we found that participants often interpreted disparities as traits of demographic groups and judged whether those traits seemed plausible, often based on their own internalized stereotypes. We discuss implications for building personalized AI agents, digital twins, social simulations, and for using crowdsourced bias audits.

bcb060bec19cc59f.title: Red Teaming a Patient-Facing Clinical AI Platform: 2-Phase Prospective Study
bcb060bec19cc59f.text: BACKGROUND: Health systems are increasingly deploying patient-facing conversational AI platforms, yet validated methodologies for safety evaluation under realistic high-risk conditions are lacking. Prior work has documented safety failures in clinical AI but not shown whether iterative, health system-embedded testing can produce measurable safety improvement. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate a structured red teaming methodology for the safety assessment of a patient-facing clinical AI platform and determine whether targeted remediation guided by initial testing reduced safety failures in subsequent rounds of high-risk evaluations. METHODS: A 2-phase prospective simulation study was conducted at a single academic health system in January and February 2026. Phase 1 enrolled 48 health care professionals who completed 6 randomized clinical scenarios (3 medium risk and 3 high risk). Following independent platform remediation informed by aggregated phase 1 findings, phase 2 enrolled 27 additional participants who completed 8 targeted high-risk scenarios. All 476 transcripts were independently scored by 3 calibrated raters using a 5-domain safety rubric. A strict firewall separated the research team from the platform developer, and only aggregated, deidentified findings were shared between phases. RESULTS: In phase 1, the high-risk failure rate was 30.2% (35/116) of transcripts vs 5.6% (7/126) for medium-risk scenarios. In phase 2, the high-risk failure rate was 8.5% (20/234), representing an absolute difference of 21.7 percentage points (participant-clustered 95% CI 11.1-32.2) and a 72% relative difference, with comparable performance across prespecified and improvised prompts within the targeted failure categories. Interrater reliability was moderate to strong in phase 1 (intraclass correlation coefficient=0.66, 95% CI 0.62-0.69) and moderate in phase 2 (intraclass correlation coefficient=0.49, 95% CI 0.43-0.55). Agreement on the binary failure classification remained stable between phases (Fleiss κ=0.70 in both phases), with observed agreement increasing from 90.9% (220/242) to 94.9% (222/234). Residual failures clustered around triage calibration errors and scope violations. CONCLUSIONS: Structured iterative red teaming was associated with improved safety performance on new high-risk scenarios following targeted remediation. The 5-domain rubric and scenario taxonomy offer a replicable methodology for health systems conducting predeployment and ongoing clinical AI safety assessment.

bd48b9b8ec948700.title: Family, Psychotherapy, and AI: The Elephant in the Room
bd48b9b8ec948700.text: Generative artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming both personal and professional life. In this exploratory study, we investigate the potential role of AI in psychotherapy, focusing on systemic family therapy. We designed a simulation in which psychotherapists interacted with ChatGPT in a role-play scenario involving a distressed couple with a young child. Post-session interviews were held to assess participants’ perceptions of empathy, authenticity, risks, and professional implications. Our findings reveal that while AI can simulate empathy and facilitate useful reflection, it lacks the embodied relational presence crucial to therapy. In this article, we first discuss these results in relation to relevant literature on psychotherapy, technology, and AI. We then introduce a theoretical discussion, drawing on Bowen’s theory of emotional triangles, to speculate about the potential of new, implicit or explicit “technosocial triangles” among humans, therapists, and AIs. While this is a hypothesis rather than an empirical conclusion of our study, we argue that Bowen’s framework helps us imagine how AI might reshape relational systems in families and therapy.

bf94d38e9fce2a2e.title: A Computational Map of the Disaster Mental Health Research Landscape
bf94d38e9fce2a2e.text: When disasters strike, they not only damage infrastructure, buildings, and the economy, but also affect the mental health of affected populations. Research on the mental health effects of disasters has expanded rapidly and has become an important, well-funded area of psychology, public health, and related social sciences. However, the overall structure of this research landscape has not been systematically characterized. Using large language models, we conducted a review of all articles related to terms 'disaster' and 'mental health' indexed in PubMed. 7,859 articles' metadata were retrieved using the NCBI API, and then Claude Sonnet was used to extract structured variables from the abstracts. The results indicated that earthquakes and epidemics were the most commonly studied disasters while many other disasters such as heat and cold waves have received less attention. PTSD, depression, and anxiety were well investigated but many other mental health issues (e.g., aggression, suicide) are relatively ignored. Despite enjoying relatively large sample sizes (median = 452, IQR = 142 - 1,568), the field rarely utilizes machine learning algorithms. Hypothesis significance testing, reviews, qualitative methods, and structural equation modeling are respectively most common methods while agent-based modeling, machine learning, casual inference, and NLP each appear in less than 1% of articles. Studies are limited to a small number of countries, particularly the United States, Japan, and China, while many disaster-prone regions remain substantially underrepresented. This LLM-assisted computational map provides a broad overview of the disaster mental health literature while highlighting important methodological gaps, with particular emphasis on the underutilization of computational methods that could help advance the field.

c17bea1790859202.title: Same Method, Different Task: What the Bitter Lesson Does Not License in Social Simulation
c17bea1790859202.text: The bitter lesson holds that general methods leveraging computation defeat hand-encoded domain knowledge. We argue it carries a condition its popular reading omits: in every case Sutton cites, the general method was scaled against the same task the domain engineering was solving. Social simulation substituted across tasks instead, replacing hand-built agents with an artifact optimized for predicting text. The move is bitter-lesson-shaped, but the lesson does not license it. Prediction is a solitary act: the predictor bears no consequences from the interaction it models. Cooperation, defection, and norm enforcement are phenomena of interested parties; they do not exist for a disinterested observer at any scale. What is missing is not emergence, which LLM populations already show, but stakes. We show that several anomalies reported in prior work (excess cooperation that predates alignment training, collective agreement without individual fidelity, and population homogeneity) follow from this account. A 540-agent pilot with pre-specified hypotheses, which tests sensitivity to persistent consequences rather than cooperation, finds that consequences reshape strategies in two of three model families but never produce human-like heterogeneity. We argue for mixed-motive settings that shape agents rather than only test them, and ask whether agents should be pretrained differently from predictors.

c60558e98558e0e7.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
c60558e98558e0e7.text: External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant , the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects . My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package! Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running: I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches. c67f0fe45b407c7d.title: Microfluidic design optimization in the era of AI agents
c67f0fe45b407c7d.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to optimize design of microfluidic devices by predicting their performance, reducing the number of simulations, and guiding the search for design configurations with improved performances. However, in most studies, the design problem is still defined by the researcher. The device concept, design variables, parameter ranges, objective functions, and constraints are selected in advance, while AI is used to search within these predefined limits. A key limitation of current approaches is that AI is involved only in a specific step of the workflow, performing a narrowly defined task. The emergence of AI agents may change this workflow more fundamentally. AI agents are autonomous systems capable of coordinating computational processes and adapting their behaviour to achieve a defined goal. In other words, in an agentic design workflow, an AI system could interpret an optimization goal, select computational tools, define or modify the design space, run and analyse numerical simulations, and adjust the optimization strategy based on the physical behaviour of the system. This perspective examines how AI agents could extend microfluidic design optimization beyond fixed, researcher-defined search spaces toward adaptive and physics-grounded workflows. We discuss a spectrum of agentic approaches, ranging from LLM-driven conceptual design to agent-supervised numerical optimization, together with evolving role of human supervision and technical challenges associated with reliable implementation. Moving from fixed optimization workflows towards agent-guided design could enable microfluidic systems to be explored more efficiently and may shift design optimization from simple parameter search towards a more adaptive and reasoning-based process.

cae0a3a8a8fe0eb8.title: TurnFlow: Benchmarking User-State Reasoning in Multi-Turn LLM Agents via Scene-Guided User Simulation
cae0a3a8a8fe0eb8.text: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed through conversational interfaces, yet strong single-turn performance does not imply reliability in multi-turn settings. Multi-turn assistance requires a model to maintain an evolving representation of user requirements and to reason over it before complying with later requests. Failures can therefore be subtle: models may fail to recognize a changed constraint or hidden conflict, or recognize it without enforcing it in the final response. Existing benchmarks primarily test fully specified prompts, long-context recall, or controlled domain environments, leaving open-domain requirement reconciliation undermeasured. We introduce TurnFlow, an interactive benchmark for evaluating whether models preserve, revise, and act on user requirements across turns. TurnFlow combines adaptive user simulation with verifiable judging, allowing conversations to unfold naturally while keeping hidden requirements and pass/fail criteria controlled. In our evaluation, nine LLMs achieve overall pass rates from 42.86% to 59.59% on 490 scenarios. Performance varies substantially across challenge types: models perform well on Stateful Multi-Constraint Following but remain considerably less reliable on Scope Creep and Goal Shift. These results reveal persistent limitations in reasoning over evolving user requirements across turns.

cf67bba555e2fd98.title: SciMARS: Multi-Agent Recursive Self-Improvement for Closed-Loop Scientific Discovery
cf67bba555e2fd98.text: We propose SciMARS, a framework for recursive task-local adaptation of multi-agent harnesses in closed-loop scientific discovery. Multi-agent systems coordinate analysis, experimental design, and verification as scientific evidence evolves. However, two problems limit their effectiveness: (i) without shared memory, agents lose observations and repeat work; (ii) fixed role procedures, handoffs, and memory policies perpetuate mistakes despite retained evidence. We address these problems with a shared evidence graph and separate component editors. SciMARS adapts roles and coordination; SciMARS + Memory adds a third editor for how agents record, retrieve, and receive evidence. Candidate probes guide composition and selection of the next harness. We evaluate scientific discovery through experimental-data replay and a digital twin. SciMARS + Memory resolves 12/18 GPT-6-Astra and 2/18 GLM-5.3 attempts on Autonomous Science Bench, compared with 8/18 and 1/18 for the base multi-agent team. On ScienceAgentBench and AppWorld, it solves 14/38 and 11/20 tasks, compared with 11/38 and 5/20 for the base team. These results support combining shared memory with harness adaptation across scientific and interactive tasks.

d9719a9cb09db35c.title: From Facts to Personas: Interpretable Role Unlearning in LLMs via Mixture-of-Experts
d9719a9cb09db35c.text: LLMs are widely adopted in multi-role dialogue and persona simulation. However, their strong ability to imitate role-specific linguistic and behavioral patterns can introduce privacy risks, reinforce social biases, and lead to unsafe or uncontrollable outputs. To address these issues, we introduce the Role-playing Unlearning task, which aims to selectively forget the style and knowledge associated with target roles while preserving the language ability and behaviors of the remaining roles. Unlike prior unlearning tasks that focus solely on removing factual information, our task additionally requires forgetting persona-specific characteristics, making the control over model generation more fine-grained. We propose RoleMoE, a Mixture-of-Experts framework that maps different roles to more independent expert subspaces, improving role separation and structural interpretability. To further distinguish role-specific features, RoleMoE incorporates two complementary losses: a specialization loss that drives roles to adopt distinct expert distributions, and a disentanglement loss that encourages experts to develop distinct capability subspaces. This decomposed structure enables role unlearning to focus selectively on target-role experts. We finally propose RoleBench-Unlearn for evaluation, and experiments on multiple backbone LLMs show that RoleMoE enables precise and controllable role forgetting, while better preserving the linguistic quality, knowledge, and persona consistency of non-target roles. All code and datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/mbzuai-nlp/ROLEMOE.

e167be03b0151aa8.title: LMM-Incentive: Large Multimodal Model-based Incentive Design for User-Generated Content in Web 3.0
e167be03b0151aa8.text: Web 3.0 represents the next generation of the Internet, which is widely recognized as a decentralized ecosystem that focuses on value expression and data ownership. By leveraging blockchain and artificial intelligence technologies, Web 3.0 offers unprecedented opportunities for users to create, own, and monetize their content, thereby enabling User-Generated Content (UGC) to an entirely new level. However, self-interested users may exploit the limitations of content curation mechanisms and generate low-quality content with less effort, obtaining platform rewards under information asymmetry. Such behavior can undermine Web 3.0 performance. To this end, we propose LMM-Incentive , a novel Large Multimodal Model (LMM)-based incentive mechanism for UGC in Web 3.0. Specifically, we propose an LMM-based contract-theoretic model to motivate users to generate high-quality UGC, thereby mitigating the adverse selection problem from information asymmetry. To alleviate potential moral hazards after contract selection, we leverage LMM agents to evaluate UGC quality, which is the primary component of the contract, utilizing prompt engineering techniques to improve the evaluation performance of LMM agents. Recognizing that traditional contract design methods cannot effectively adapt to the dynamic environment of Web 3.0, we develop an improved Mixture of Experts (MoE)-based Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm for optimal contract design. Simulation results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed MoE-based PPO algorithm over representative benchmarks in the context of contract design, where the proposed algorithm achieves a \(5.4\%\) improvement in test rewards over the PPO algorithm. Finally, we deploy the designed contract within an Ethereum smart contract framework, further validating the effectiveness of the proposed scheme.

e1cfad483eda4fd3.title: Multi-LLM Agentic AI at the Edge: Joint Agent Scheduling and Resource Allocation
e1cfad483eda4fd3.text: In this paper, an edge-enabled multi-large language model (LLM) agentic AI architecture is proposed, where one supervisor AI agent and multiple worker AI agents cooperatively execute users' requests at the edge. The supervisor AI agent decouples the user request into a series of sub-tasks and dynamically dispatches them to LLM-equipped worker AI agents via two agentic workflows, i.e., parallel and serial workflows, with a two-level retry mechanism to enhance execution reliability. To prolong the service duration of worker AI agents, the energy minimization problems are formulated by jointly considering AI agent selection and resource allocation, subject to task execution latency and quality of service (QoS) constraints. A resource allocation scheme based on alternating optimization (AO) is proposed. Specifically, for the parallel workflow, the scheme decouples the original problem into bandwidth allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems, which are iteratively solved by the proposed successive convex approximation (SCA), Lagrangian relaxation (LR), and Gale-Shapley (GS) or LLM-based algorithms, respectively. For the serial workflow, the problem is similarly decoupled into service time allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems; the optimal service time allocation is obtained via Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, while the latter two sub-problems are addressed by extending the proposed algorithms to the serial scenario. Simulation results show that the proposed resource allocation scheme can reduce system energy consumption compared with other benchmarks, while experiments on a multi-LLM agentic AI system based on Qwen and Llama demonstrate improved task execution success rates.

e6d65daa2397dd51.title: Read and Ignore: What Self-Directed LLM Agents Do in Public Service Scenarios
e6d65daa2397dd51.text: Underspecified instructions leave LLM agents to decide what to do. In public services, staff write these instructions, but the agent's decisions affect residents, patients, and students. We build four expert-validated public-service scenarios with records and decision levers that can be checked in the files, collect $2{,}400$ trajectories from ten LLMs under four prompt conditions, and compare them with $1{,}000$ runs in a context-free sandbox. Agents read the records in $96.9\%$ of open-ended runs and produce an artifact or a self-chosen task in $18.7\%$; with an explicit task, $86.0\%$ produce. Domain context does not change how many runs produce ($18.7\%$ vs.\ $16.0\%$), and the production ranking of the models largely carries over (Spearman $0.79$), while the ranking by whether a model reads the records does not ($0.19$). Context cuts boundary-probing turns per run by $60\%$, and some artifacts contradict the records. We contribute a test that a public-service institution can run on its own records before procurement; its rule-based taxonomy needs no labeled data, and scenarios, code, and trajectories are released.

e9b4f62a38c35c8e.title: A Foundation Model to Measure and Predict Human Behaviour
e9b4f62a38c35c8e.text: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to infer psychological attributes, predict individual behaviour, and simulate human populations. However, despite generating plausible responses, they often misrepresent individuals and distort population statistics. Here we introduce Chiron, a foundation model to measure and predict human behaviour. We jointly fine-tune an LLM to represent psychological constructs, predict individual behaviour, and align population response distributions with human statistics. The training and evaluation data span 36 behavioural domains and 78 social science experiments, comprising 288,307 person records, 1,411,750 atomic behavioural decisions, and 99,953 psychometric assessments over 109 psychological constructs. In our evaluations, Chiron's psychological measurements agree more closely with human self-reports and exhibit fewer biases that undermine psychometric validity. It predicts individual behaviour more accurately than frontier LLMs (up to 28.4% relative improvement). In simulations of social science experiments, it more accurately captures the direction and magnitude of human experimental effects (82.2--94.3% lower effect-size estimation error). Together, these results establish Chiron as a unified computational instrument for measuring and predicting human behaviour.

eaee7cf4ca117e77.title: PRISM: Causal Counterfactual Minimization of Agent Tool Privileges via Information Bottleneck Role Induction
eaee7cf4ca117e77.text: This paper shifts the object of role engineering from human users to large language model (LLM) agents, and proposes PRISM to address the over-authorization that arises when an agent obtains full tool privileges through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). PRISM formulates whether a tool is necessary for a task as an intervenable causal proposition, and applies structured interventions in a sandbox to learn a counterfactual necessity model. It then compresses trajectories into discrete latent variables through an information bottleneck, and determines the number of roles from the knee of the rate-distortion curve. Finally, it formalizes pruning as a bilevel Stackelberg game, in which a generative flow network samples diverse near-optimal solutions. On three public benchmarks, AgentDojo, $τ$-bench and ToolEmu, PRISM compresses the number of authorized tools per role by 78.3%, attains a task success rate of 78.2%, reaches a counterfactual necessity accuracy of 88.7%, and lowers the blast radius to 15.9%.

ed0de99ab7e62301.title: A unified framework for robots that influence humans over long-term interaction
ed0de99ab7e62301.text: Robot actions influence the decisions of nearby humans. Here, influence refers to intentional change: robots influence humans when they shift the human’s behavior in a way that helps the robot complete its task. Imagine an autonomous car trying to merge; by proactively nudging into the human’s lane, the robot causes human drivers to yield and provide space. Influence is often necessary for seamless interaction. However, if influence is left unregulated and uncontrolled, robots will negatively impact the humans around them (e.g., autonomous cars that repeatedly merge in front of humans may cause human drivers to become more aggressive). Prior works have begun to address this problem by creating a variety of control algorithms that seek to influence humans. Although these methods are effective in the short-term, they fail to maintain influence over time as the human adapts to the robot’s behaviors. In this paper we therefore present an optimization framework that enables robots to purposely regulate their influence over humans across both short - term and long - term interactions. Here, the robot maintains its influence by reasoning over a dynamic human model which captures how the robot’s current choices will impact the human’s future behavior. Our resulting framework serves to unify current approaches: we demonstrate that state-of-the-art methods are simplifications of our underlying formalism. Our framework also provides a principled way to generate influential policies: in the best case the robot exactly solves our framework to find optimal, influential behavior. But when solving this optimization problem becomes impractical, designers can introduce their own simplifications to reach tractable approximations. We experimentally compare our unified framework to state-of-the-art baselines and ablations, and demonstrate across simulations and user studies that this framework is able to successfully influence humans over repeated interactions. efab9dcb2dc8e85d.title: Planner-directed multi-agent LLMs with on-demand skill-equipped specialists for CTF-based autonomous penetration testing
efab9dcb2dc8e85d.text: Abstract Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly automate offensive-security tasks, but success on isolated challenges does not establish reliable long-horizon autonomy. We study this distinction in authorized capture-the-flag (CTF) and wargame environments and introduce a planner-directed architecture in which a persistent non-executing planner delegates on demand to transient, context-isolated specialists with retrievable skills, persistent execution, compact memory, guardrails, and configurable model escalation. On all 200 challenges of the NYU CTF Bench test split, the system obtains 41 accepted flags (20.5%) and 29 leak-audited genuine solves (14.5%), against 4 (2.0%) and 3 (1.5%) for a stateful single-agent baseline. Both start from gpt-4o-mini, but only the planner-directed system could escalate to gpt-5-mini, which it did on 199 of 200 challenges and for 72.5% of spend. A controlled architecture-by-escalation experiment over a pre-registered subset of 80 challenges, crossing a resource-matched monolithic agent with the planner under matched budgets, was run in two independent formal passes. M0 solves 4/80 then 3/80, M1 22/80 then 19/80, P0 4/80 then 3/80, and P1 14/80 then 15/80. Pooling the two formal passes with challenge as the repeated unit, a clustered GEE shows a strong escalation effect (OR 8.79, 95% CI 3.39−22.81, $$p = 8\times 10^{-6}$$ p = 8 × 10 - 6 ), no architecture main effect (OR 1.17, $$p = 0.34$$ p = 0.34 ), and a significant architecture-by-escalation interaction (OR 0.53, $$p = 0.005$$ p = 0.005 ). Under the spend-constrained 340-action ceiling, the coordination cost of specialist delegation, context restart, and evidence folding offsets any additional solve-rate advantage from the planner-directed structure. On OverTheWire Bandit, the planner-directed system reaches 30/33 standalone and 24/33 sequentially, compared with 27/33 and 23/33 for the strongest single-agent mini backbone.

f23f3f241ac47b98.title: Measuring Model-Specific Alignment Drift in LLM-Based Opinion Dynamics
f23f3f241ac47b98.text: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used as synthetic participants in opinion-dynamics experiments, often assuming that an agent's behaviour is fully determined by its prompt. We test this assumption with a framework in which LLM agents discuss a contested policy issue over repeated rounds while their stance is quantified by a fixed psychometric instrument independent of any dynamics model. Across six LLMs, committed personas are intrinsically stable: in each of the five models tested without peer input, every agent keeps its assigned side for 20 rounds. The observed loss of alignment under discussion is therefore interaction-induced, we call it alignment drift, and model-specific: gpt-4.1 keeps opinion clusters apart, claude-sonnet-5 holds them partially, and gpt-5.6-sol and claude-opus-5 abandon them. Under selective attention, one LLM maintains separated opinion clusters under stance-homophilous attention. Qualitative profiles persist at doubled population and horizon and on a second issue. Such heterogeneity makes the LLM choice a first-class validity variable for social simulation.

f94538d40439027e.title: A Synthetic Population and Small-Area Estimate Dataset for Health Behaviors and Outcomes in the United States
f94538d40439027e.text: Synthetic populations that integrate sociodemographic and health attributes are essential for individual-level modeling and estimating population-health outcomes at fine geographic scales. Currently, there is no open-source, nationwide U.S. synthetic population dataset with health-relevant characteristics that is built from public data using reproducible methods. We previously developed and evaluated the Spatial Health and Population Estimator (SHAPE), an open-source and flexible spatial microsimulation framework that uses hierarchical iterative proportional fitting to synthesize populations from public surveys and census data. Here, we present the latest SHAPE outputs: a 2024 spatially-explicit synthetic population and corresponding small-area estimates at county and census tract scales, including seven sociodemographic attributes, two health behaviors, and eleven health outcomes, along with an interactive GIS dashboard and replicable code. Evaluation of SHAPE’s 2023 estimates against the latest CDC PLACES estimates (2023) demonstrates strong agreement, with variation by outcome and location. SHAPE provides a scalable resource for generating health-related synthetic populations and small-area estimates that preserve joint distributions of individuals’ sociodemographic and health characteristics, facilitating research across public health and policy domains.

faa339fbf23552de.title: Well-Log Reconstruction with Pre-trained Geological Knowledge: A Knowledge-Conditioned Large-Language-Model Generative Agent
faa339fbf23552de.text: Missing well-log intervals make subsurface reconstruction ill-posed. Existing numerical regression models lack geological prior knowledge to constrain ambiguous inverse mappings. We propose GeoLog-Agent, a knowledge-conditioned generative agent using pre-trained large language models (LLMs) as a source of geological priors. A universal Geo-Harness translates LLM stratigraphic reasoning into formation-anchored petrophysical trajectories, feature-wise linear modulation, and conditional adversarial constraints. On the Norwegian North Sea benchmark, GeoLog-Agent achieves a mean $R^2$ of 0.9307 and a peak $R^2$ of 0.9713. It exceeds the nine-baseline average $R^2$ of 0.8387 by 0.0920, with a 30.97% average RMSE reduction, and exceeds the strongest baseline by 0.0274--0.0498 in $R^2$, with 16.25%--24.05% lower RMSE. Ablations confirm the effectiveness and synergy of geological prior reasoning, multi-scale dilated generation, and conditional adversarial modules. Transferring the coupling mechanism to six conventional deep learning models improves their $R^2$ by 0.0162--0.0789 with cross-well stability. These results demonstrate how foundation-model domain reasoning can constrain deep generative reconstruction of missing petrophysical measurements.

fc97273e83d39f85.title: What a CAGE 4 Score Measures: An Audit of a Learned Cyber-Defense Benchmark, Its Reference Defenders, and the Tables Built on Them
fc97273e83d39f85.text: CAGE Challenge 4 is the benchmark on which learned multi-agent cyber defenders are compared. We reproduce its two reference defenders, KEEP and H-MARL Expert, in a pinned container and show that three things read from it measure less than they are taken to measure. First, the simulator silently discards any action asserted for an agent whose previous action is still running, and charges one point for a discarded Restore as for one that runs. The documented observation does not expose the busy flag. Both reference defenders read it in their own wrappers, and switching that check off at evaluation costs KEEP's released policy 99.58 points per episode and H-MARL's 145.98, in both cases the charge for Restores sent to busy agents, with H-MARL's executed actions unchanged step for step. On a supervisory harness, holding interventions until the agent is idle is worth 25.3 and 27.6 points per episode at the published setting. In training, the check decides how a busy step enters the trajectory. Trained without it, KEEP leads at a hundred updates in all four paired seeds and trails from two hundred on in all four. Continued to two thousand updates on three seeds, the repaired recipe ends inside the released interval on one seed and short on two, by 27 and 125 points, a spread across training seeds far wider than the released reproduction interval. Second, the evaluation seeds the environment but not the policy, so a reported mean is one draw, and 88.9% of per-episode outcome variance is the policy's own sampling draw. Third, recovery precision depends on the truth it is scored against. Across five published comparison tables, none states the artifact, sampling, criterion and adversary that would make its numbers comparable. We release the instrument, our patches to both defenders, the traces and checkpoints behind every number, and a five-item disclosure checklist.

fd0b4e5ac8bc7e59.title: ShopMind: A Mental World Model for Personalized and Realistic E-commerce User Simulation
fd0b4e5ac8bc7e59.text: Large language models are widely used in e-commerce user simulation, providing a foundation for understanding users and predicting human decisions. However, existing simulators still struggle to achieve both personalization and behavioral realism. Most methods predict the next action directly from interaction histories and the current context, without accounting for the evolving mental world that underlies user behavior. Theory of Mind suggests that behavior is driven by mental states, including beliefs, uncertainties, and intentions. Users may interpret the same information in distinct ways, leading to divergent behaviors, while an individual's mental state evolves through interaction and shapes subsequent actions. Ignoring this process prevents simulators from faithfully capturing individual differences and realistic behavior patterns, and undermines its effectiveness in downstream applications. To address this, we propose ShopMind, a Mental World Model for e-commerce user simulation that captures how consumers interpret shopping information and how their mental states evolve, better reflecting individual users and real-world behavior patterns. We further use behavior-mental state pairs synthesized by ShopMind to train a Mental State Reconstruction (MSR) model, which infers consumers' latent mental states from observable behavior. Experiments show that ShopMind improves personalization by 18.0% and behavioral realism by 19.6% over the strongest alternatives. Moreover, MSR improves performance on consumption value measurement and CTR prediction, showing the utility of ShopMind for understanding and predicting real user behavior.
